findings.claim: All 42 practice questions across lessons 1-7 label the Shakespeare tasks “15 marks — Extract Response” (14 of them) and “25 marks — Essay Response” (14 of them), and every band ladder is built on those totals (Top band 13–15 and 21–25). The remaining 14 are the house “4 marks — Quote Analysis” short questions. Several ladders are also mislabelled internally, repeating “Top band” for the second and third rungs (lessons 2–7).
findings.truth: Edexcel Section A is a two-part question worth 20 + 20. Part (a) is 20 marks, AO2 only, on a printed extract of about 30 lines. Part (b) is 20 marks, AO1 15 + AO3 5, on how a theme from the extract is explored elsewhere in the play. There is no 15 + 25 split, and no AO4 or spelling mark on this section. Relabelled to 20 marks each and the ladder rebuilt as 17–20 / 13–16 / 9–12 / 5–8 / 1–4, matching the sister Edexcel Shakespeare units.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md lines 1102-1113 (two-part question; part a) close language analysis of a ~30-line extract, AO2; part b) how a theme from the extract is explored elsewhere in the play, AO1 and AO3; 80 marks; 1h45; closed book) and the raw-mark table at lines 1312-1350 (Questions 1a-6a: AO2 20; Questions 1b-6b: AO1 15 + AO3 5)

findings.claim: All seven part (b) stems copy another board's formula: “Starting with this extract, explore how Shakespeare presents … Write about the extract and the play as a whole.” None of them names the extract it starts from.
findings.truth: Edexcel part (b) does not ask students to write about the extract again. It states what the extract shows, then asks how that theme is explored elsewhere in the play. Rewritten to that shape and pointed at the extract set by the part (a) question above it.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md line 1108: “Part b) is focused on how a theme from the extract is explored elsewhere in the play”; also line 438

findings.claim: “his brother Antonio, ‘in my trust,’ conspired with Alonso, King of Naples, to overthrow him” — “in my trust” is presented as Prospero's words.
findings.truth: The phrase does not occur in the play. Prospero says “and my trust, / Like a good parent, did beget of him / A falsehood in its contrary, as great / As my trust was; which had indeed no limit, / A confidence sans bound.” Replaced with the real quotation “a confidence sans bound.”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042 lines 429-433 (Act 1, Scene 2); “in my trust” returns no match in the play text

findings.claim: “Antonio never speaks in the final scene's reconciliation” (lesson 3, repeated in its flashcard “He never speaks”) and “while Alonso repents, Antonio says nothing” (lesson 6, with a matching knowledge check).
findings.truth: Antonio does speak in Act 5: “Very like; one of them / Is a plain fish, and no doubt marketable” — a sneer at Caliban. What he never does is reply to Prospero's forgiveness. The lessons now say that instead, so the ‘silence’ reading survives without the false plot claim.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042, Act 5 Scene 1, Antonio's speech at line 265 of the scene (file line 3647); no other Antonio speech heading appears after the Act 5 heading

findings.claim: Gonzalo's utopia is quoted as one continuous speech: “No sovereignty — / All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavour.”
findings.truth: Sebastian (“Yet he would be king on't”) and Antonio speak between the two halves. An ellipsis now marks the cut so a student does not reproduce it as a single run of verse.

findings.claim: The renunciation is quoted as “Some heavenly music — which even now I do — / I'll break my staff”.
findings.truth: Two lines are cut without a mark: “To work mine end upon their senses that / This airy charm is for”. An ellipsis now marks the cut.

findings.claim: The mark scheme for the question “how Shakespeare uses the concept of ‘the Other’ in Prospero's characterisation of Caliban” says “Caliban is labelled ‘savage,’ ‘monster,’ ‘thing of darkness’”.
findings.truth: Prospero never calls Caliban a monster. All 44 uses of ‘monster’ in the play belong to Stephano and Trinculo (plus one unrelated simile from Antonio). Prospero's words are ‘savage’, ‘slave’, ‘a born devil’ and ‘this thing of darkness’, so the mark scheme now reads ‘born devil’.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042: every ‘monster’ line (1898-3121) sits under _Ste._ or _Trin._; “A devil, a born devil” is Prospero at line 3063 (Act 4, Scene 1)

findings.claim: Flashcard: “Which Gonzalo line gets Prospero's warmest praise in Act 5?” with the answer “Holy Gonzalo, honourable man.”
findings.truth: That line is Prospero's, about Gonzalo, not a line spoken by Gonzalo. The question now asks which line shows Prospero's praise for Gonzalo.

findings.claim: Lessons 1, 2, 6 and 7 all state that Prospero taught Caliban language (“Prospero teaches Caliban language”; the flashcard “Caliban using Prospero's language against him”).
findings.truth: Editions disagree. The Folios give the ‘Abhorred slave … I pitied thee, / Took pains to make thee speak’ speech to Miranda; Theobald (after Dryden) reassigned it to Prospero, which is what the Cambridge text used here prints. Arden 3, Oxford and several classroom editions restore it to Miranda. A student who writes ‘Miranda taught him’ is also defensible, so nothing is edited, but the same phrasing probably recurs across the other Shakespeare units.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042 line 814 (_Pros._ Abhorred slave) with the textual note at line 1186: “351: Pros.] Theobald (after Dryden). Mira. Ff.”

findings.claim: “set adrift in a ‘rotten carcass of a butt’ — a barely seaworthy boat”, and the matching flashcard gloss ‘an unseaworthy boat’.
findings.truth: The quotation is right for the Folio and for modern editions (Arden, Oxford), so it stays. The gloss is loose: a ‘butt’ is a cask, as Stephano's ‘butt of sack’ later in the play shows. The Cambridge text used here prints the 19th-century emendation ‘boat’, which is why the gloss reads that way. Not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #23042 line 500 (“A rotten carcass of a boat”) and lines 2007, 2024, 2320 (Stephano's ‘butt’ = cask)

summary: Every quotation in the seven lessons is verbatim and correctly placed, and the context checks out (Bermuda 1609 and the Sea Venture, Strachey, the 1611 court performance, Montaigne's ‘Of Cannibals’ rather than More's Utopia, Iris/Ceres/Juno, Gonzalo's charity). The unit's main fault is board-wide: all 28 Shakespeare practice questions and their band ladders sit on a 15 + 25 split where Edexcel is 20 + 20, and all seven part (b) stems use another board's ‘write about the extract and the play as a whole’ formula. Four smaller faults are real: a fabricated ‘in my trust’ quotation, the claim that Antonio never speaks in Act 5 (he does — he calls Caliban marketable), ‘monster’ attributed to Prospero, and two quotations that hide an omission. No banned strings and no spec codes anywhere in the unit.
